newsitem.title: USA: US still not issuing grain export certs for Turkey.
newsitem.headline: US still not issuing grain export certs for Turkey.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Department is still not issuing any phytosanitary certificates for grains or oilseed exports to Turkey, a USDA spokesman said Wednesday.

The official said that despite Turkey's recent agreement to allow grain shipments into the country with 0.05 percent ergot fungus content, Turkey is still insisting on zero-tolerance levels for six other diseases that USDA says it cannot guarantee.

"Right now, Turkey would like us to certify that the grain is free of a number of diseases that we can't guarantee it is free of," said an official with USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service.

"The ergot issue has been settled, but there's still other problems remaining...there are no (phytosanitary certificates) for any type of grains (and oilseeds) being issued to Turkey," said the official.

Turkey was originally insisting that Washington guarantee zero content level for a number of bacterial and fungal diseases. That list has been whittled down to six diseases Turkey is most concerned about.

Diseases that Turkey is still maintaining a zero-tolerance level for are: Flag Smut, Black Chaff, TCK smut, Barley Stripe Mosaiic Virus, Septoria Nodorum and Cochliobulus Victoriae (known in the United States as bipolaris victoriae).
The USDA official said U.S. and Turkish plant quarantine officials are in discussions, and that hopefully the issue will be resolved soon.
"Right now we're consulting with them and talking about those diseases and seeing what we can do and what accommodation we can do. But there's no break yet," he said.
"We just can't make the promise that grain is free of all traces of those diseases," he added.
The official said about 85,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat in port at Turkey cannot be unloaded until the problem is settled.

In a teleconference from Rome with reporters Wednesday, Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said he got the impression from his last week's meeting with the Turkish ambassador that Turkey would be changing its import regulations fairly soon to come more in line with international norms.

"I got the clear impression that since the Turkish position was so outside the international norm on sanitary and phytosanitary standards that we would likely see some sort of a change fairly soon, but I have not discussed it any further since then," Glickman said.
